title: Why Is One Nostril ALWAYS Blocked? 👃
description:
You pinch one nostril shut... and the other one is blocked. Relax: that's not a cold, your nostrils work in shifts, and that one is on its break. Subscribe for a new strange question every day.

How it works: the inside of your nose is lined with spongy tissue that can fill with blood. One side swells and nearly shuts its passage while the other shrinks and opens wide, and every few hours they swap. It is called the nasal cycle. It was first measured in 1895, and in a 2016 study that tracked 33 people's breathing for a day everyone had it: a shift lasted about two hours on average, but anything from 15 minutes to 10 hours. You mostly notice it with a cold, when everything in there is already swollen. Why the nose does it is not settled; one idea is that each side gets to rest and stay moist. And because one nostril has fast air and the other slow, each smells the world a little differently: in a 1999 study in Nature, the same mix of a minty smell and a fuel smell seemed mintier through the fast nostril and more like fuel through the slow one. A nostril that is blocked all the time, or always on the same side, is one for a doctor.
